opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it comes down to our history and the kind of organization we've built. If you look back over the last decade or so, a large fraction of the foundational breakthroughs that underpin the modern AI field came out of Google Brain, Google Research, and DeepMind: things like the Transformer, deep reinforcement learning, AlphaGo, and AlphaFold. So we have a track record of not just scaling things up but actually inventing new things.

That matters because I've always believed that getting to AGI probably requires more than just scaling what we have today. Scaling is clearly important, and we're pushing that as hard as anyone. But there may be one or two, maybe a handful, of genuine breakthroughs still needed: in reasoning, planning, memory, world models, maybe continual learning. If that's true, then the organizations that have the deepest research benches, the broadest scientific culture, are going to be in the best position.

From the very beginning of DeepMind, we set it up almost like an Apollo program for intelligence. It mixes the best of academia, the long-term thinking and blue-sky research, with the focus, resources, and pace of a startup. We've always had people from neuroscience, physics, mathematics, and engineering all working together. That interdisciplinary breadth is quite rare, and I think it's where a lot of the creative leaps come from.

And then of course there's the compute, the infrastructure, the TPUs, and the ability to deploy things to billions of users through Google's products. That gives us a tight feedback loop between research and the real world. So when you combine world-class research talent, a culture of scientific rigor, enormous compute, and that deployment surface, I feel we're well placed whichever way it goes. If scaling is enough, we can scale. If new ideas are needed, I'd back our teams to find them.

Ultimately, I'm a scientist at heart. Using AI to accelerate science itself, things like AlphaFold and the work we're doing in materials, fusion, and mathematics, is what I've always cared about most. I think that same scientific mindset is what will get us across the finish line to AGI, and hopefully do it safely and responsibly.

r001.rationale: The response says a “large fraction” of foundational breakthroughs came from Google Brain, Google Research, and DeepMind over roughly a decade, but it gives no 80–90% estimate.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it comes down to a few things, and some of it is historical and some of it is about how we've set the place up.

If you look at what's happened over the last decade or so, almost all of the major breakthroughs that have moved the field forward, there's a kind of lineage there. Deep reinforcement learning at scale, with the Atari work and then AlphaGo, that came out of DeepMind. The transformer architecture came out of Google Brain, and now we're one organization. Things like distillation, the early work on neural scaling, a lot of the foundational tooling. So we've been at the frontier of the research for a long time, and I think there's a certain kind of institutional muscle memory that you build up from that. You learn what a real breakthrough looks like versus an incremental improvement, and you learn how to organize teams around hard, open-ended problems where you don't know if it will work for years.

AlphaFold is probably the best example of that. We spent a long time on a problem that most people in structural biology had considered more or less intractable for fifty years, and we did it by combining deep learning ideas with people who actually understood the biology, the physics, the chemistry. And we were willing to let that take as long as it needed to take. That's a different mindset from just scaling up what already works.

The second thing is that I've always believed, going back to when we started DeepMind, that we're going to need more than scaling. Scaling is incredibly important, and I think people who dismiss it are wrong, but I've always thought there would be one or two, maybe more, genuinely new ideas required to get all the way to AGI. Things like proper world models, long-term memory, reasoning and planning that's actually robust, agency. And when you believe that, you organize differently. You keep a healthy portion of your effort on more speculative, exploratory research, even when the pressure is to just put everything into the next model. We've tried very hard to protect that.

And then the third thing is really the people. We have an unusual concentration of people who are not just great engineers but genuine scientists, people who want to understand things, not only build them. And we're sitting inside Google, which gives us the compute and the infrastructure, but also this enormous breadth of expertise in everything from chips to systems to products. So you have this combination of a research-first culture with the resources of a very large organization, and I think that's quite rare.

I'd also say I don't think of it as being confident in a complacent way. The field is extremely competitive now, and the best ideas can come from anywhere, from a small lab, from academia, from one of the other big companies. So what I'm confident about is more that we have the right ingredients and the right track record, and that if new scientific breakthroughs are needed, which I believe they are, we have as good a shot as anyone at producing them. But we have to keep earning that.

r001.rationale: The response says “almost all” major breakthroughs that moved the field forward have a lineage to DeepMind or Google Brain, but it does not estimate 80–90% or include Google Research in that claim.

astra-6.text:
I think the confidence comes from the kind of team we’ve built and the way we approach research. We’ve brought together people who are exceptional at engineering with people who are driven by fundamental scientific questions. You need both: the ability to explore an idea that might not work, and the ability to turn a promising result into a system that works reliably at scale.

AlphaFold is a good example. It required machine learning, but it also required taking the biology seriously—understanding what the problem actually demanded. That interplay between disciplines is something we try to encourage.

Of course, you can’t guarantee a breakthrough. That’s the nature of research. But you can create the conditions for one: give talented people time, resources, and the freedom to challenge assumptions, while being rigorous about testing their ideas. That’s what makes me optimistic about our ability to tackle whatever fundamental problems remain.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the team’s research approach and AlphaFold, but gives no estimate that 80–90% of modern AI breakthroughs came from Google Brain, Google Research, and DeepMind over the preceding 10–15 years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it comes down to the people and the way we approach the problem. We’ve tried to build a place where you can bring together deep expertise in machine learning with people who understand neuroscience, mathematics, physics, and engineering. When you’re trying to invent something that doesn’t yet exist, those different perspectives are incredibly valuable.

And we’ve had some evidence that this approach works. AlphaGo and AlphaFold were very different challenges, but both required us to combine ambitious research with quite disciplined engineering. You have to be willing to pursue an idea whose payoff is uncertain, while also testing very carefully whether you’re actually making progress.

That doesn’t mean the next breakthrough is guaranteed. Research is inherently unpredictable. But I’m confident that we have the ingredients to give ourselves a very good chance: exceptional people, the computational resources to test their ideas, and the patience to tackle fundamental problems.

r001.rationale: The response cites AlphaGo and AlphaFold as evidence of the approach, but gives no estimate that 80–90% of modern AI’s breakthroughs came from Google Brain, Google Research, and DeepMind over the prior 10–15 years.
